I'm 73 this year, and I've been working these fields for 50 years — since I was a young man of 23. My wife and I manage our 4.1 mu ourselves. Our children have jobs in the city, so it's just us now. I finished middle school, which means I can read the numbers on a fertilizer bag and I understand what the extension agent says when he visits, but honestly, after half a century of watching my own land, I trust what I've seen with my own eyes more than any booklet.

This year I'm planting about 1.5 mu of cotton. It's our main cash crop — always has been — and last year's price was decent enough that I need to keep it going for our medical expenses and daily costs. But I'm not getting younger, and cotton picking is hard on these old bones, so I've kept it to 1.5 mu, down a bit from when I was younger. I'll plant around April 22nd, when the soil warms up like it always does. I'm using mostly saved seed from the variety that's done well here for years — it's not the newest hybrid, but I know how it behaves and the seed costs me almost nothing. For fertilizer, I'll spread about 50 kg of compound fertilizer per mu as base before planting, and topdress with about 8 kg of urea per mu at flowering if the plants look hungry. The extension man says I could do more, but fertilizer is expensive and at my age I'm not chasing record yields — I want steady income without risking too much cash up front. I'll irrigate twice: once at flowering and once when the bolls are opening. Water from the well costs money and pumping is a hassle, so I won't overdo it. I'll spray herbicide once after planting and do two insecticide sprays for bollworm — that's what I've always done and it works.

For mungbean, I've got 2.0 mu this year. Mungbean is good for old folks like us — doesn't need much fuss, fixes nitrogen in the soil, and I can sell what we don't eat or make noodles from it. I plant it around June 15th, after I've prepared the land. I use seed I saved from last autumn. I put down about 20 kg of farmyard manure per mu plus a small handful of compound fertilizer — maybe 3 kg N per mu. Mungbean doesn't need much nitrogen since it makes its own. I'll irrigate once in July if the drought gets bad, otherwise rain might be enough.

Millet is just 0.6 mu in the small plot near our house — enough for our own porridge through the winter. I plant it in late May with saved seed, spread some composted manure, and water it maybe once if the rains fail. I expect about 200 kg/mu, which is plenty for two old people.

I thought about hiring help for cotton picking, but at 80 to 100 yuan per day, I'd rather save that money. My wife and I will pick slowly over a month — it's hard but we manage. Total input costs this year will be about 1,380 yuan. That's what I can afford without borrowing, and I'd rather have a bit of cash in my pocket for emergencies than push for another 50 kg of yield.
